screens.title: Configuring and Monitoring Spanning Tree Protocol on Junos
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol on Juniper EX switches, and why it matters for predictable Layer 2 topology. You will learn how to enable RSTP on Junos, influence the Root Bridge election using bridge priority, tune port cost to prefer specific paths, and enable security features that prevent rogue devices or link failures from creating loops. We'll also walk through the operational show commands you need to verify state and troubleshoot when convergence is unexpected. The practical emphasis is on safe changes: make a lab change, verify timers and roles, and watch the effect on Root Port and Designated Port selection. For example, you will set a low bridge priority so a switch becomes the Root Bridge, change a port cost to steer traffic, and enable BPDU Guard on access interfaces so a rogue device cannot inject BPDUs and destabilize the domain. Throughout the screens I will point out common mistakes, like inconsistent priorities or forgotten security settings, and offer short checks you can run before committing. By the end you should understand configuration commands, how to read key show outputs, and how to protect your Layer 2 network against accidental or malicious topology changes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these screens you will be able to enable and tune Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol on Junos EX switches, interpret operational outputs, and protect your Layer 2 topology. First, you will configure RSTP and confirm it is active with the relevant show commands. Next, you will influence the topology by setting bridge priority and port costs so traffic uses preferred paths; you will practice choosing priority values and cost values appropriate for link speeds. You will also enable and validate essential STP security features such as BPDU Guard, Loop Protection, and Root Protection to stop rogue devices and prevent loops. Finally, you will learn troubleshooting steps and safe verification practices so changes do not cause outages. Each objective couples a configuration action to a verification or safety check so you can practice in a lab and then apply the same checks in production with confidence. You will also encounter brief scenarios to predict Root Port selection after a cost change and to verify that a port goes error-disabled when a BPDU is received on an edge port. These skills reduce risk and lead to more predictable Layer 2 behaviour.

screens.title: Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol on Junos
screens.narratorSegment: Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol is the modern evolution of STP designed for faster convergence after topology changes. On Juniper EX switches RSTP (802.1w) is commonly enabled by default because it reduces the time a network spends in transitional states and restores forwarding faster than classic 802.1D. Enabling RSTP on Junos is straightforward: the command sets the protocol globally and commit applies it. Practically, enabling RSTP means the switch will exchange BPDUs with neighboring switches and participate in Root Bridge elections and port role assignments. A common misconception is that enabling RSTP alone fixes all convergence problems; in fact, RSTP speeds state transitions, but predictable results require thinking about which switch should be the Root and about port costs so traffic flows where you expect. A short example command sequence from the switch config is: set protocols rstp and commit. After that, use show spanning-tree bridge to confirm the Root and timers. The key takeaway is that RSTP gives you quicker recovery, but you must pair it with intentional topology design and verification to avoid unexpected path selection or outages. Ask yourself: after enabling RSTP, have you verified the Root Bridge and critical port roles in your domain?

keyIdea.title: RSTP basics
keyIdea.text: RSTP reduces convergence time, but still needs active design: enable it and verify Root and port roles.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.4 › RSTP Overview
Definition
RSTP (802.1w) provides faster port role transitions and improved convergence after a topology change compared to legacy STP.
Commands to enable RSTP (lab example): 
set protocols rstp
commit
Why this matters: Faster convergence reduces blackholes and speeds recovery when links flap or devices reboot.
Misconception: Turning on RSTP alone does not control Root selection or path costs — you must configure priority and costs for predictable results.
Key Takeaway

Enable RSTP to gain faster convergence, then verify the Root and port roles with show commands before making further topology changes.

Concrete example
In a lab, enter the set protocols rstp command and commit. Next run show spanning-tree bridge to confirm the local switch and the elected Root Bridge IDs and timers. If the Root is not the switch you expect, plan a bridge-priority change rather than leaving the setup ambiguous.
Check your understanding
Why might enabling RSTP still leave traffic using a suboptimal path? Answer: because bridge priority and port costs determine which switch and port are preferred; RSTP alone does not set those preferences.

screens.title: Root Bridge and Bridge Priority
screens.narratorSegment: The Root Bridge is the focal point of the spanning tree: all path costs are measured relative to it. Junos uses a bridge priority value combined with the MAC address to form the Bridge ID; lower values win the election. Juniper defaults to 32768, and priorities are configured in increments of 4096 — for example 0, 4096, 8192, and so on. To force a specific switch to be Root, set its bridge-priority to a lower value than the rest of the domain; a typical lab command is set protocols rstp bridge-priority 4k. A practical example: if all switches use the default 32768 and you set one switch to 4096, that switch will have the lowest Bridge ID and will be chosen as Root. A common misconception is that the switch with the lowest MAC automatically becomes Root; in fact priority is evaluated first, then MAC as a tiebreaker. Another important consideration is consistency: if you lower a priority on one switch but forget to make complementary changes on other devices, you might get unexpected Root changes during maintenance. After setting priority, commit and immediately check show spanning-tree bridge on multiple switches to verify the election. Think: who should be the Root to minimize transit across your core VLANs?

keyIdea.title: Root selection
keyIdea.text: Lower bridge-priority values win Root election; use multiples of 4096 to make results predictable.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.4 › Root Bridge & Priority
Bridge Priority rules
Priorities are configured in multiples of 4096; lower numerical priority has higher election preference.
Command example
# To make this switch the Root Bridge
set protocols rstp bridge-priority 4k
commit
Default priority is 32768. Setting a lower value like 4096 ensures this switch wins unless another switch has an even lower priority.
Misconception check: The MAC address only breaks ties; do not rely on MAC ordering for predictable topology.
Concrete scenario
Imagine a core pair where you want a specific unit to be the Root to centralize forwarding. Set its priority to 4k, commit, and run show spanning-tree bridge on both switches. Confirm the chosen Root ID and that your planned uplinks are Root Ports on non-root switches.
Common mistake

Changing priority on one switch without checking other switches can cause unintended Root changes during failovers. Always verify across the domain.

screens.title: Port Cost and Path Selection
screens.narratorSegment: Port cost is the second lever you use to influence which path a switch chooses to reach the Root Bridge. RSTP prefers lower cost paths when selecting Root Ports and Designated Ports. Juniper switches assign default costs based on interface speed — common defaults include 20,000 for 100 Mbps, 2,000 for 1 Gbps, and 200 for 10 Gbps. If you have two uplinks to the same Root and want traffic to prefer the higher-speed 10 Gbps link, ensure that link has a lower cost either through the default assignment or by manually setting the cost on the other link to a higher value. The configuration command is set protocols rstp interface cost. A concrete example: set protocols rstp interface ge-0/0/0 cost 100 will make that port more preferred than a port with cost 200 or 2,000. A common misconception is expecting port speed alone to determine selection when manual costs or non-default defaults are present. After you set costs, run show spanning-tree interface to verify the role and resulting forwarding state. Always document manual cost changes so future operators understand why a non-default cost was set and which path was intended to carry traffic.

keyIdea.title: Port cost matters
keyIdea.text: Lower port cost steers path selection; set costs deliberately and verify port roles after changes.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.4 › Port Cost
Default cost examples
Typical default Juniper costs: 20,000 for 100 Mbps, 2,000 for 1 Gbps, 200 for 10 Gbps. Use manual costs to override defaults where necessary.
Manual cost command
# Set explicit cost for an interface
set protocols rstp interface ge-0/0/0 cost 100
commit
Example: To prefer a 10 Gbps link, ensure it has a lower cost than any competing path. If a competing 1 Gbps uplink has cost 2000, setting the 10 Gbps port to 200 will prefer it.
Misconception check: Do not assume physical speed always wins; configured costs or defaults may change preference.
Comparison — two uplinks
Uplink A
Speed: 10 Gbps
Cost: 200
Uplink B
Speed: 1 Gbps
Cost: 2000
With these costs, the switch will prefer Uplink A to reach the Root. If you manually increase A's cost above B, the preferred path will flip. After changes, run show spanning-tree interface on both ports to confirm role and state.

screens.title: CLI: Setting Port Cost and Verifying Roles
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll walk through the practical commands to set a port cost and then verify how the switch uses that information when selecting roles. First, enter configuration mode and set the cost on the interface you want to influence. For example, set protocols rstp interface ge-0/0/0 cost 100 and commit. That command changes the cost that RSTP uses to evaluate path selection. After committing, use show spanning-tree interface ge-0/0/0 to inspect the port's role — you should see whether it is Root, Designated, Alternate, or Boundary — and its state, such as Forwarding or Blocking. If the port became the preferred path, it will be in the Forwarding state and may be chosen as Root Port on a non-root switch. A common misconception is thinking the change takes effect only after a reboot; in reality, RSTP recalculates topology promptly after commit. A concrete example: you lower ge-0/0/0 cost to 100 and the competing link has cost 2000 — the switch will prefer ge-0/0/0. If the result is not what you expect, check for spanning-tree priorities on neighboring switches and ensure no manual costs override your plan. Finally, document and test the change in a lab, then run the show spanning-tree statistics command to review BPDU counts and ensure the network is exchanging expected control traffic.

keyIdea.title: Verify after change
keyIdea.text: After changing cost, confirm the port role and state with show spanning-tree interface and check BPDU stats.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.4 › Port Cost — CLI Walkthrough
Commands
edit
set protocols rstp interface ge-0/0/0 cost 100
commit

# Verify the port role and state
show spanning-tree interface ge-0/0/0

# Review BPDU activity
show spanning-tree statistics
The edit and commit steps apply configuration immediately. Use show commands to confirm how RSTP recalculated roles.
Interpreting interface output
  • Role: indicates Root, Designated, Alternate, or Boundary.
  • State: Forwarding or Blocking tells you whether the port carries traffic.
  • Cost: shows the configured or default cost used in calculations.
Pro tip: If results differ from expectation, inspect neighbor priorities and costs. A remote lower priority can still make a different Root.

screens.title: BPDU Guard (bpdu-block-on-edge)
screens.narratorSegment: BPDU Guard is a protection mechanism for edge or access ports that should never receive BPDUs from connected devices. When enabled, if an access port receives a BPDU, the port is immediately transitioned to an error-disabled or blocked state, preventing a rogue switch from influencing the spanning tree topology. On Junos this feature is configured per interface with set protocols rstp interface ge-0/0/3 bpdu-block-on-edge, or enabled globally for all edge ports with set protocols rstp bpdu-block-on-edge. A concrete lab exercise: configure an access port with BPDU Guard, then connect a test device that sends BPDUs. The protected port should move into an error-disabled like state, showing that BPDUs were blocked. A common misconception is treating BPDU Guard as a troubleshooting tool rather than a preventive control — it is intended to stop harmful BPDUs at the edge, not to debug topology problems. After a BPDU Guard event, recovery may be required using device-specific recovery commands. For production, always document which ports have BPDU Guard and pair this setting with monitoring so you can quickly identify and remediate legitimate misconfigurations versus malicious attempts.

keyIdea.title: BPDU Guard purpose
keyIdea.text: BPDU Guard blocks ports that receive unexpected BPDUs, protecting the STP topology from rogue switches.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.4 › BPDU Guard
Configuration examples
# Enable on a specific access interface
set protocols rstp interface ge-0/0/3 bpdu-block-on-edge
commit

# Or enable globally for edge ports
set protocols rstp bpdu-block-on-edge
commit
When a protected port receives a BPDU, it is taken out of forwarding to prevent topology changes introduced by a connected device.
Scenario
You have an access port for an employee workstation. Enabling BPDU Guard ensures that if someone plugs in an unmanaged switch, that port will not allow the new device to affect the spanning tree.
Recovery note
After an edge port is disabled due to BPDU reception, you will need to follow recovery steps or clear the recovery-mode state to return the port to service.

screens.title: Loop Protection
screens.narratorSegment: Loop Protection helps prevent a non-edge port from transitioning to forwarding if it stops receiving BPDUs, which could otherwise create a loop. This feature is useful on trunk links between switches where BPDUs might be dropped because of congestion or a unidirectional failure. On Junos you enable loop protection on an interface with set protocols rstp interface ge-0/0/2 loop-protection and commit. When loop protection detects that BPDUs are no longer received, it moves the interface into a loop-inconsistent (blocking) state rather than allowing it to forward. This behaviour prevents the formation of temporary loops that are often catastrophic on Layer 2 networks. A common misconception is that loop protection is only for poorly designed networks; in reality it provides a safety net for transient BPDU loss on critical trunks. After enabling this protection, monitor show spanning-tree interface to see when a port is loop-inconsistent. Also include this setting in your design notes, because blocking a trunk has operational consequences and may require a planned restoration sequence. In short: loop protection is a defensive control that sacrifices a link rather than risking a broadcast storm.

keyIdea.title: Loop Protection purpose
keyIdea.text: Block trunks from forwarding when BPDUs are lost, preventing loops from unidirectional failures or dropped control traffic.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.4 › Loop Protection
Command example
# Enable loop protection on a trunk
set protocols rstp interface ge-0/0/2 loop-protection
commit
If a port with loop protection stops receiving BPDUs, it transitions to loop-inconsistent and stays blocking to avoid forming a loop.
Practical notes
Use loop protection on trunks and inter-switch links where BPDU loss could cause an alternate port to start forwarding. Document such settings and monitor interfaces so you can respond if a trunk is intentionally blocked.
Pro tip: If a trunk becomes loop-inconsistent, investigate the reason for missing BPDUs — it may indicate a unidirectional fault or severe congestion affecting control plane traffic.

screens.title: Root Protection
screens.narratorSegment: Root Protection is a defensive STP feature that ensures an already-elected Root Bridge remains the Root. When configured on a designated port, if that port receives a superior BPDU indicating a better Root candidate, the port transitions to a root-inconsistent blocking state rather than allowing the new Root election to proceed via that port. On Junos you enable root protection per interface with set protocols rstp interface ge-0/0/1 root-protection and commit. Use this on designated ports that should never become Root Ports, for example on access-facing uplinks where another switch might attempt to supplant the Root. A common misconception is treating Root Protection as a replacement for intentional root-design; it is a safeguard for accidental or malicious attempts to influence Root selection. After enabling, monitor show spanning-tree interface for root-inconsistent states and decide on manual remediation steps if a legitimate Root change is required. In operational practice, pair root protection with a documented Root priority plan: set the intended Root with a low bridge-priority and enable root protection on other designated ports to keep the topology stable during maintenance or misconfiguration events.

screens.title: Monitoring RSTP — Key show Commands
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring RSTP is essential to confirm that your configuration produced the expected topology and to troubleshoot problems. The three most useful show commands described in the chapter are show spanning-tree bridge, show spanning-tree interface, and show spanning-tree statistics. Use show spanning-tree bridge to view global RSTP information including the Root Bridge ID, local bridge ID, and timers; this tells you which device is currently Root and whether timers are default or adjusted. Use show spanning-tree interface on a specific port to see that port's role — Root, Designated, Alternate, or Boundary — and its state such as Forwarding or Blocking, plus its configured cost. This command helps you confirm which physical link carries traffic after a change. Use show spanning-tree statistics to inspect BPDU counts sent and received; unusually low BPDU reception may indicate a one-way failure or congestion that could trigger Loop Protection. A practical workflow is to run these commands after any priority or cost change and then compare outputs across neighboring switches to ensure a consistent view. A common mistake is querying only the local switch; always check both ends of a link. Ask: do both ends agree on the role and cost? If not, recheck configuration and physical link health.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safe Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter highlights several common mistakes that lead to surprises in RSTP domains. One mistake is inconsistent bridge priorities across devices: if you intend a specific Root but forget to set a low priority on all primary candidates, the election can move unexpectedly during maintenance. Another frequent issue is incorrect port cost settings, causing suboptimal paths; if a critical uplink retains a high cost, traffic may traverse a slower or unwanted route. Forgetting to enable STP security features on access or trunk ports is also common—without BPDU Guard, a rogue switch can inject BPDUs and disrupt the topology. For troubleshooting, follow a safe step-by-step process: first run show spanning-tree bridge to confirm the Root, then show spanning-tree interface on affected ports and check show spanning-tree statistics to validate BPDU activity. If a port is in an inconsistent or error-disabled state, check the specific protection feature (for example, BPDU Guard or Loop Protection) that may have triggered the change, and follow the vendor recovery steps. Always test changes in a lab and document pre-change state so you can roll back. The final practical check: after making any change, confirm that forwarding paths still meet your performance and resilience goals.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough: Make SW1 the Root and Enable BPDU Guard
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on scenario walks you through making a Juniper EX switch named SW1 the Root Bridge and securing an access port with BPDU Guard. Begin in configuration mode and ensure RSTP is enabled. Then set SW1's bridge priority to a low value such as 4k to make it the Root Bridge. Configure the access port ge-0/0/0 for your VLAN and enable bpdu-block-on-edge on that interface. Commit the configuration and run show spanning-tree bridge on SW1 and a neighboring switch to verify SW1 is the Root. Next run show spanning-tree interface ge-0/0/0 to confirm the access port role and that bpdu-block-on-edge is effective. To test BPDU Guard, attach a test device that sends BPDUs to ge-0/0/0; the port should transition to an error-disabled or blocked state. If the port goes down, follow the recovery steps described in your device documentation, such as clearing the ethernet-switching recovery-mode, to bring the interface back. A common mistake during this exercise is forgetting to commit after each change; always commit and then verify. This lab reinforces the pairing of configuration with verification and recovery planning so you can deploy the same steps in production with confidence.

edit

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol on Juniper EX switches, and why it matters for predictable Layer 2 topology. You will learn how to enable RSTP on Junos, influence the Root Bridge election using bridge priority, tune port cost to prefer specific paths, and enable security features that prevent rogue devices or link failures from creating loops. We'll also walk through the operational show commands you need to verify state and troubleshoot when convergence is unexpected. The practical emphasis is on safe changes: make a lab change, verify timers and roles, and watch the effect on Root Port and Designated Port selection. For example, you will set a low bridge priority so a switch becomes the Root Bridge, change a port cost to steer traffic, and enable BPDU Guard on access interfaces so a rogue device cannot inject BPDUs and destabilize the domain. Throughout the screens I will point out common mistakes, like inconsistent priorities or forgotten security settings, and offer short checks you can run before committing. By the end you should understand configuration commands, how to read key show outputs, and how to protect your Layer 2 network against accidental or malicious topology changes.

By the end of these screens you will be able to enable and tune Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol on Junos EX switches, interpret operational outputs, and protect your Layer 2 topology. First, you will configure RSTP and confirm it is active with the relevant show commands. Next, you will influence the topology by setting bridge priority and port costs so traffic uses preferred paths; you will practice choosing priority values and cost values appropriate for link speeds. You will also enable and validate essential STP security features such as BPDU Guard, Loop Protection, and Root Protection to stop rogue devices and prevent loops. Finally, you will learn troubleshooting steps and safe verification practices so changes do not cause outages. Each objective couples a configuration action to a verification or safety check so you can practice in a lab and then apply the same checks in production with confidence. You will also encounter brief scenarios to predict Root Port selection after a cost change and to verify that a port goes error-disabled when a BPDU is received on an edge port. These skills reduce risk and lead to more predictable Layer 2 behaviour.

These objectives center on hands-on confidence and safety. You will execute the lab sequence to make a switch the Root Bridge and then test that change with the show commands. You will practice applying BPDU Guard on edge ports so a misconnected device cannot alter topology, and you will learn to enable Loop Protection on trunk ports to avoid forwarding when BPDUs are lost. You will also be guided through root-protection so designated ports cannot accept a superior BPDU and allow a rogue Root. Importantly, you will pair each configuration with verification commands and safe rollback or recovery steps. For example, after enabling bpdu-block-on-edge, you'll intentionally send a BPDU from a test device to confirm the port enters an error-disabled or blocked state and then practice the recovery command. Each objective emphasizes lab verification first, then cautious deployment in production. This reduces the risk of accidental outages while giving you predictable behavior in larger networks.

Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol is the modern evolution of STP designed for faster convergence after topology changes. On Juniper EX switches RSTP (802.1w) is commonly enabled by default because it reduces the time a network spends in transitional states and restores forwarding faster than classic 802.1D. Enabling RSTP on Junos is straightforward: the command sets the protocol globally and commit applies it. Practically, enabling RSTP means the switch will exchange BPDUs with neighboring switches and participate in Root Bridge elections and port role assignments. A common misconception is that enabling RSTP alone fixes all convergence problems; in fact, RSTP speeds state transitions, but predictable results require thinking about which switch should be the Root and about port costs so traffic flows where you expect. A short example command sequence from the switch config is: set protocols rstp and commit. After that, use show spanning-tree bridge to confirm the Root and timers. The key takeaway is that RSTP gives you quicker recovery, but you must pair it with intentional topology design and verification to avoid unexpected path selection or outages. Ask yourself: after enabling RSTP, have you verified the Root Bridge and critical port roles in your domain?

The Root Bridge is the focal point of the spanning tree: all path costs are measured relative to it. Junos uses a bridge priority value combined with the MAC address to form the Bridge ID; lower values win the election. Juniper defaults to 32768, and priorities are configured in increments of 4096 — for example 0, 4096, 8192, and so on. To force a specific switch to be Root, set its bridge-priority to a lower value than the rest of the domain; a typical lab command is set protocols rstp bridge-priority 4k. A practical example: if all switches use the default 32768 and you set one switch to 4096, that switch will have the lowest Bridge ID and will be chosen as Root. A common misconception is that the switch with the lowest MAC automatically becomes Root; in fact priority is evaluated first, then MAC as a tiebreaker. Another important consideration is consistency: if you lower a priority on one switch but forget to make complementary changes on other devices, you might get unexpected Root changes during maintenance. After setting priority, commit and immediately check show spanning-tree bridge on multiple switches to verify the election. Think: who should be the Root to minimize transit across your core VLANs?

Port cost is the second lever you use to influence which path a switch chooses to reach the Root Bridge. RSTP prefers lower cost paths when selecting Root Ports and Designated Ports. Juniper switches assign default costs based on interface speed — common defaults include 20,000 for 100 Mbps, 2,000 for 1 Gbps, and 200 for 10 Gbps. If you have two uplinks to the same Root and want traffic to prefer the higher-speed 10 Gbps link, ensure that link has a lower cost either through the default assignment or by manually setting the cost on the other link to a higher value. The configuration command is set protocols rstp interface cost. A concrete example: set protocols rstp interface ge-0/0/0 cost 100 will make that port more preferred than a port with cost 200 or 2,000. A common misconception is expecting port speed alone to determine selection when manual costs or non-default defaults are present. After you set costs, run show spanning-tree interface to verify the role and resulting forwarding state. Always document manual cost changes so future operators understand why a non-default cost was set and which path was intended to carry traffic.

Now we'll walk through the practical commands to set a port cost and then verify how the switch uses that information when selecting roles. First, enter configuration mode and set the cost on the interface you want to influence. For example, set protocols rstp interface ge-0/0/0 cost 100 and commit. That command changes the cost that RSTP uses to evaluate path selection. After committing, use show spanning-tree interface ge-0/0/0 to inspect the port's role — you should see whether it is Root, Designated, Alternate, or Boundary — and its state, such as Forwarding or Blocking. If the port became the preferred path, it will be in the Forwarding state and may be chosen as Root Port on a non-root switch. A common misconception is thinking the change takes effect only after a reboot; in reality, RSTP recalculates topology promptly after commit. A concrete example: you lower ge-0/0/0 cost to 100 and the competing link has cost 2000 — the switch will prefer ge-0/0/0. If the result is not what you expect, check for spanning-tree priorities on neighboring switches and ensure no manual costs override your plan. Finally, document and test the change in a lab, then run the show spanning-tree statistics command to review BPDU counts and ensure the network is exchanging expected control traffic.

BPDU Guard is a protection mechanism for edge or access ports that should never receive BPDUs from connected devices. When enabled, if an access port receives a BPDU, the port is immediately transitioned to an error-disabled or blocked state, preventing a rogue switch from influencing the spanning tree topology. On Junos this feature is configured per interface with set protocols rstp interface ge-0/0/3 bpdu-block-on-edge, or enabled globally for all edge ports with set protocols rstp bpdu-block-on-edge. A concrete lab exercise: configure an access port with BPDU Guard, then connect a test device that sends BPDUs. The protected port should move into an error-disabled like state, showing that BPDUs were blocked. A common misconception is treating BPDU Guard as a troubleshooting tool rather than a preventive control — it is intended to stop harmful BPDUs at the edge, not to debug topology problems. After a BPDU Guard event, recovery may be required using device-specific recovery commands. For production, always document which ports have BPDU Guard and pair this setting with monitoring so you can quickly identify and remediate legitimate misconfigurations versus malicious attempts.

Loop Protection helps prevent a non-edge port from transitioning to forwarding if it stops receiving BPDUs, which could otherwise create a loop. This feature is useful on trunk links between switches where BPDUs might be dropped because of congestion or a unidirectional failure. On Junos you enable loop protection on an interface with set protocols rstp interface ge-0/0/2 loop-protection and commit. When loop protection detects that BPDUs are no longer received, it moves the interface into a loop-inconsistent (blocking) state rather than allowing it to forward. This behaviour prevents the formation of temporary loops that are often catastrophic on Layer 2 networks. A common misconception is that loop protection is only for poorly designed networks; in reality it provides a safety net for transient BPDU loss on critical trunks. After enabling this protection, monitor show spanning-tree interface to see when a port is loop-inconsistent. Also include this setting in your design notes, because blocking a trunk has operational consequences and may require a planned restoration sequence. In short: loop protection is a defensive control that sacrifices a link rather than risking a broadcast storm.

Root Protection is a defensive STP feature that ensures an already-elected Root Bridge remains the Root. When configured on a designated port, if that port receives a superior BPDU indicating a better Root candidate, the port transitions to a root-inconsistent blocking state rather than allowing the new Root election to proceed via that port. In operational practice, pair root protection with a documented Root priority plan: set the intended Root with a low bridge-priority and enable root protection on other designated ports to keep the topology stable during maintenance or misconfiguration events.
